overview: This atlas label appears from 1920 to 1938, but its outline mainly covers Laos and Cambodia; Hanoi, Hue and Saigon fall outside it under separate Vietnamese labels. The historical French federation was wider. Read this card as a guide to that colonial system and its varied communities, with each example located rather than treated as one uniform culture.

periods.title: Formation before the mapped interval
periods.summary: An 1887 decree united French-controlled territories under a governor-general. Laos joined the colonial framework after the 1893 agreement with Siam.

periods.title: The first atlas snapshot
periods.summary: The map begins a narrow Laos-and-Cambodia outline, while separate Annam and Cochin China labels represent Vietnamese territories.

periods.title: Learning and colonial pressures
periods.summary: Buddhist institutes opened in Vientiane in 1931 and Luang Prabang in 1933, combining religious scholarship with colonial political aims.

periods.title: After the label disappears
periods.summary: The map stops this label before Japanese wartime intervention, the French return and the struggles that dismantled colonial rule.

items.text: French Indochina was an administrative federation, not an ancient nation. The 1911 decree distinguished Cochinchina, ruled as a colony, from the protectorates of Annam, Tonkin, Cambodia and Laos. It also listed the leased Chinese territory of Quang-Tchéou-Wan. A single umbrella name therefore concealed several different legal arrangements.

The governor-general supervised civil services and defense. Local governors and senior residents could receive delegated powers, while customs, post and telegraph services helped tie the territories together. Colonial officials claimed authority over societies with their own rulers, institutions and histories; the decree describes the rulers’ machinery, not popular consent.

Phnom Penh, Vientiane, Luang Prabang and Angkor lie inside this record’s sampled outline. Vietnamese examples below belong to the wider federation even though their cities lie outside this polygon. The dates 1920 and 1938 mark an atlas label change, not the federation’s founding and independence.

sections.title: Food, households and the work behind colonial roads

items.text: For Rmeet communities described as Lamet in an ethnography based on 1937 to 1938 fieldwork in northern Laos, rice farming organized much more than dinner. Shifting fields, the agricultural calendar and religious activities connected households and extended families. People exchanged labor, making a harvest a matter of cooperation between neighbors as well as work within one home.

Road building also had a coercive side. Historian Geoffrey Gunn documents colonial public works using corvée, compulsory labor, in Laos in 1934, including roads and river communications. These projects drew on people’s time and effort; a new transport route was not simply a gift from the administration. Official accounts also recorded noncooperation by the population.

sections.title: Cambodian makers and a museum full of lessons

items.text: Phnom Penh’s new museum opened on 13 April 1920 during Khmer New Year, with King Sisowath present. Its temple-inspired building stood beside a school of Cambodian arts. Students, teachers and practicing craftspeople helped carry skills forward: the museum was connected to making things, not just looking at them behind glass.

Visitor Harriet Winifred Ponder’s 1936 account credits eight master craftsmen and ten pupils with carving the museum’s large central door in 45 days. A doorway could therefore be a shared workshop project and an architectural showpiece. The makers deserve a place in the story alongside the French designer.

Ponder described pupils entering at about fifteen and beginning with drawing before choosing crafts such as woodcarving, metalwork or sculpture. Her account places girls in weaving classes. This is evidence for one specialist school and its gender divisions, rather than the timetable of every Cambodian child.

A Cambodian woman taught weaving at her own handloom while pupils practiced simpler designs. Ponder estimated that one small sampot on the teacher’s loom took about a fortnight. Making a patterned garment was slow, skilled work: decidedly longer than choosing clothes from a cupboard!

sections.title: Books, schools and voices of their own

items.text: The Buddhist Institute in Vientiane opened in February 1931. Prince Phetsarath chaired it, and scholar Sila Viravong served as secretary. Sila compiled or translated teaching materials including grammars, Buddhist stories and chants. These were active Lao intellectual projects within a colonial institution, not knowledge arriving only from France.

Religious education also carried political arguments. French officials wanted to redirect Lao monks’ educational links away from Siam and toward Phnom Penh. Scholars in Laos could object to being treated as subordinate to Cambodia. A schoolbook’s language and place of publication could become questions of cultural authority.

In the 1930s, some Vientiane monks reportedly obtained printed Lao stories from northeastern Thailand and copied them onto palm leaves for circulation. New printing and older manuscript skills worked together. A printed book did not instantly send the handwritten book into retirement.

In 1935, Sila Viravong compiled a four-volume Lao grammar under the Buddhist Institute. In Cambodia, presses also issued Khmer-language religious, official and secular material. Different scripts required suitable printing type, while the price of printing and a small readership limited Lao book production.

In Saigon, outside this record’s outline but inside the wider colonial federation, the women’s newspaper Phụ Nữ Tân Văn began on 2 May 1929. Its weekly pages debated education, careers and women’s ability to build independent lives. Such arguments challenged expectations about women’s roles in families and public life.

A short writing sample is the newspaper’s Vietnamese title, “Phụ Nữ Tân Văn”, translated by the ISEAS Library as “Women’s Gazette”. It is already written in the Latin-based quốc ngữ script, so no separate transliteration is needed. This is a Saigon publication from 1929 onward, not a common language shared by all Indochina.

Saigon’s Pasteur Institute opened in 1891 under Albert Calmette, with a mission to provide vaccination against rabies and smallpox. This medical center belonged to the wider federation beyond the displayed outline. Its foundation records an important service, but does not tell us that every village or family could reach it.

In Hanoi in 1902, before this atlas interval, new sewers offered rats sheltered places to breed. Historian Michael Vann traced the resulting extermination campaign through colonial archives. Infrastructure intended to make a city healthier had also created excellent rat accommodation. This is a city-specific sanitation story, not evidence of universal piped toilets.

The authorities paid a bounty for rat tails. According to Vann’s archival investigation, they then discovered tailless rats and rat farms supplying the reward scheme. Paying for a tail was clearly not the same thing as proving a rat population had fallen! The episode exposes a badly designed policy rather than a model to copy.

In Laos, investigations of the Plain of Jars were another interwar development. Madeleine Colani reported a funerary interpretation in 1932, drawing on finds including pottery, ornaments and beads. These huge stone containers belonged to a much earlier past. Archaeologists were investigating ancient communities, not discovering monuments made by the colonial state.

The label’s disappearance in 1938 was not liberation. Japanese forces entered Indochina in 1940 while a French administration loyal to Vichy continued functioning. Japan overthrew that administration on 9 March 1945. French efforts to reestablish control after Japan’s defeat met independence movements, and war broke out in Vietnam in 1946.

Laos’s transition came in stages. Its 1949 arrangements made it an associated state within the French Union; the treaty of 22 October 1953 explicitly recognized full independence and sovereignty. That distinction matters: a new constitutional label and the transfer of full powers were not necessarily the same event.

ending.text: Cambodia achieved full independence in November 1953, and the Geneva settlement of July 1954 marked the end of French Indochina. Its peoples did not disappear with the colonial framework: Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam followed distinct national paths, and conflict continued beyond this card’s story.
